# Sampling and digital transmission (pulse-code modulation) (`sampling_pcm`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: helped by binary_numbers, vacuum_tube, information_theory, telephone, sound_recording, semiconductors_transistor, error_correcting_codes
- Core idea: A continuous signal such as speech can be turned into numbers without loss that matters. Measure it at regular instants more than twice as often as its highest frequency (8,000 times a second for telephone speech up to 3,400 vibrations per second) and the original can be rebuilt exactly from the samples. Round each sample to one of a fixed number of levels, for example 256, which is eight binary digits, and send the digits as on/off pulses. A repeater then only has to decide whether a pulse is present and send a fresh clean one, so noise and distortion do not add up along the line as they do with amplifiers, and the stream can be stored, switched, enciphered and combined with others. The price is bandwidth: 64,000 bits per second for one uncompressed telephone channel.
- Pitfalls:
  - Sampling too slowly or without first filtering off the higher frequencies: they reappear as false low tones
  - Too few levels, which gives a harsh background noise; and equal steps for speech, where finer steps for quiet sounds work much better
  - Judging it wasteful because of the bandwidth; the gain is that a poor, noisy line can regenerate pulses while they are still distinguishable, though errors remain possible
  - Attempting it with valves on a large scale; it became economic only with transistors
- History: europe: 1915 – Whittaker's interpolation theorem; 1933 Kotelnikov states the sampling theorem for communication; 1937–1938 Alec Reeves invents pulse-code modulation at the ITT laboratory in Paris; americas: 1928 – Nyquist's result on pulses and bandwidth; 1943 SIGSALY, an enciphered digital speech link for the Allied leaders (Bell Labs); 1948 Oliver, Pierce and Shannon, The Philosophy of PCM; 1962 T1 digital telephone carrier; east_asia: 1949 – Someya's independent statement of the sampling theorem in Japan
- Read:
  - B. M. Oliver, J. R. Pierce & C. E. Shannon, The Philosophy of PCM, Proceedings of the IRE 36 (1948)
  - Claude E. Shannon, Communication in the Presence of Noise, Proceedings of the IRE 37 (1949)
